newsitem.title: UK: Halifax banks on life in British FTSE elite.
newsitem.headline: Halifax banks on life in British FTSE elite.

text.p: Britain's banking landscape changed dramatically on Monday when former building society Halifax Plc shot into third place among the banks listed on the London stock market.

Halifax -- ditching 144 years of mutuality in favour of the rigours of life as a publicly-quoted company -- joined the elite of Britain's top 100 quoted firms with a market capitalisation of more than 18 billion pounds ($29.5 billion).
This makes it Britain's third largest bank, behind Lloyds TSB and HSBC, which owns Midland Bank but marginally ahead of Barclays Plc and some way beyond NatWest.
Halifax's flotation follows the trail blazed in April by its smaller rival Alliance & Leicester which made its stock exchange debut with a market capitalisation of 3.3 billion pounds.
The first building society to opt for life as a bank was Abbey National which made the change in 1989 and has since proved to be an innovative competitor in the banking and savings market.
Other mutually-owned building societies -- Britain's traditional lenders to homeowners -- are also planning to follow the same route.
Northern Rock and the Woolwich are both due for flotation while another society Bristol & West is being taken over by the Bank of Ireland.
Building societies are owned by their members, the savers and borrowers, who have received substantial windfall payments for voting to convert their societies to publicly listed companies.

Analysts say Halifax will give the high street banks a run for their money, capitalising on its retail focus and its cash surplus of more than three billion pounds, enabling it to make strategic acquisitions to boost its performance.

The competition to expand the range of services offered by Britain's banks, in the face of stiff competition from non-traditional sources such as supermarkets, is set to become even more fierce as avenues for expansion and cross-selling dry up.

Lloyds TSB is the benchmark for British personal financial services and several institutions have tried to challenge its pre-eminence in the sector. BZW analyst Timothy Sykes believes Halifax could be a significant competitive threat to the firm.
This view is echoed by Goldman Sachs banking analyst David Townshend who believes Halifax "will be a leader in the financial services industry in the long run", while warning of short term risks.

Richard Coleman,, banking analyst at Halifax's corporate broker Merrill Lynch, told a telephone news conference he would be surprised if Halifax continued to trade at a significant premium to Lloyds TSB.
With a prospective price/earnings multiple -- a benchmark for establishing the growth prospects of a company -- of over 17 times, Halifax would rank above Lloyds TSB and its other peers.

But analysts do not expect the new bank's shares to maintain the sort of levels they have seen on their debut, buoyed as they have been by demand from institutional investors, pension funds and insurance companies, desperate for a piece of the action.
Merrill Lynch corporate broker James Agnew said the dealing in the shares had got off to a good start and had resulted in a "reasonable but not excessive premium" for the shares.

Agnew said 200 institutions, largely British but some from overseas, had bid successfully for the 23 percent of Halifax shares sold on Friday. But there had been a good balance of retail and institutional buying on the first day of trading, he added.
Halifax may have become the latest member of an exclusive club of British banks, but it leaves behind a dwindling but feisty group of building societies.
For by deserting their building society roots, the Halifax and the other converting societies have opened a widening gulf in approach between them and those pledged to mutuality.

At the annual meeting of the Building Societies Association last month, the remaining societies trumpeted the benefits of remaining mutual which they said would mean lower rates for borrowers and higher savings rates for investors.

They argue that converting societies, while willing to hand out generous one-off windfalls, will be tied to the demands of producing ever increasing profits for their City masters and this will result in poorer rates for their customers.
At the average auction price achieved for Halifax members of 732.5 pence a share, the firm said eligible savers and borrowers with an average 330 share allocation will net 2,417 pounds.
A total of 7.6 million Halifax members are to become shareholders as a result of its flotation.
The shares were trading at 738 1/29 at 1514 GMT, down from an initial opening price of 774.5 pence and a high of 788 pence. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
